strengths: Introduces the first multiview, real-world benchmark (SceneDiff) with instance-level, per-object change annotations across substantially different viewpoints, filling a clear gap relative to prior benchmarks that either assume near-duplicate viewpoints or only provide per-view/semantic labels (Table 1 comparison is thorough and convincing).

The training-free SceneDiff method is well-motivated, combining off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction (π³), segmentation (SAM), and appearance (DINOv3) models via an asymmetric geometry-consistency score plus region-level appearance matching; the design choices (bidirectional visibility masks, asymmetric depth-difference rule, region-based rather than pixel-based matching) are sensible and clearly derived from failure modes of naive pixelwise comparison.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results on the new SceneDiff benchmark (per-view/per-scene/AP_type), on the existing two-view RC-3D benchmark, and on ChangeSim, with large margins over baselines (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, a VLM+GroundingSAM pipeline).

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analysis in the supplement: contribution of each score term, comparison across geometry backbones (π³, VGGT, DUSt3R, Fast3R) and feature extractors (DINOv1/2/3), robustness to dynamic content, threshold sensitivity, and detailed failure-case analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, low-overlap geometry failure, strong lighting) — this level of self-critical analysis is unusually strong and adds credibility.
Concrete downstream demonstration (robot tidying task) shows practical utility beyond benchmark numbers.

Clear annotation tool/protocol description and evaluation protocol (per-view, per-scene, per-scene-type AP) with illustrative figures, supporting reproducibility; commitment to release code, tool, and data.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest (e.g., 46.3 per-scene AP, 25.5 AP_type on SD-V; even lower on SD-K), and the paper's own failure analysis shows the method degrades substantially under cluttered/repetitive scenes, low view overlap, and strong lighting changes — the task is explicitly stated as unsolved, which somewhat limits the immediate impact/reliability of the method for real applications despite outperforming baselines.

The method is entirely training-free and built on several large pretrained foundation models (π³, SAM, DINOv3); this makes performance and reproducibility contingent on the continued availability/behavior of these external models, and the pipeline is fairly heavy (159s/pair, Table 6), which may limit practicality for real-time robotic use cases the paper motivates.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably fair-minded (e.g., feeding regressed depth to CYWS-3D, adjusting 3DGS-CD sampling rate), could still be seen as somewhat favorable to the proposed pipeline since SceneDiff's own geometry/segmentation backbones are strictly stronger/more modern than what baselines were originally designed with; a more apples-to-apples ablation (e.g., baselines given the same π³ geometry) is only partially explored.

Dataset collection process (350 pairs from a guideline-driven, apparently small pool of contributors capturing casual videos) is not fully detailed in terms of number of annotators/contributors, potential biases in scene selection, or inter-annotator agreement for mask/label quality, which could affect diversity claims and annotation reliability.

The evaluation protocol (point-based matching with up to two tolerated extra detections per GT, dynamic entropy thresholding, oracle-comparable) is reasonable but somewhat permissive/complex, and its sensitivity to design choices (e.g., allowed FP tolerance) is not deeply analyzed relative to how it affects reported AP numbers.

The paper does not report variance/uncertainty (e.g., multiple runs, confidence intervals) given some stochasticity in thresholding and model outputs, nor statistical significance of the reported improvements over baselines.

strengths: Introduces the first instance-level, multiview object change detection benchmark (SceneDiff) with 350 diverse real-world video pairs across 20 scene categories, indoor and outdoor, with dense object instance annotations — filling a clear gap relative to prior semantic/pixel-level or similar-viewpoint benchmarks (well summarized in Table 1).

Proposes a training-free method built by composing pretrained geometry (π³), segmentation (SAM), and semantic feature (DINOv3) models, enabling generalization across domains without retraining and the ability to improve as underlying foundation models advance.

Extensive empirical validation across four benchmarks (proposed SceneDiff, RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim) with consistent, sizable improvements over strong and diverse baselines (pixel-level, box-level, 3DGS-based, and VLM-based), along with thorough ablations of geometry and feature backbones.

Commendable transparency: detailed failure-case analysis (cluttered/repetitive scenes, geometry reconstruction failure under low overlap, strong lighting changes), hyperparameter sensitivity studies, and robustness checks (dynamic content masking, alternative geometry models) that clarify the boundaries of applicability rather than only showcasing favorable results.

Practical downstream demonstration via a real robotic tidying application, plus a well-documented SAM2-based annotation tool that reduces annotation time, supporting reproducibility and future dataset extension.

Careful, well-justified adaptation of baseline methods (CYWS-2D/3D, 3DGS-CD, MV3DCD, VLM+SAM3) to the new benchmark, with supplementary analysis showing these adaptations do not unfairly disadvantage baselines.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains quite low even for the proposed method (e.g., obj/sc AP of 22.8/10.8, obj/im AP of 43.8/23.6 on the two SceneDiff subsets, and near-zero scores in the change-type-aware and cluttered-scene settings), indicating the task is far from solved; this is appropriately acknowledged but tempers the practical impact claims.

The method's core novelty is mainly in composing and scoring with existing pretrained components (3D reconstruction, SAM segmentation, DINOv3 features) rather than a new representation or learning approach; the individual technical modules (reprojection scoring, region matching, greedy association) are relatively standard.

The overall pipeline is heavily bottlenecked by the pretrained 3D geometry model — failure analysis shows that limited view overlap causes total reconstruction/detection failure, and different geometry backbones (e.g., VGGT) can invert static/moved object dynamics, raising concerns about robustness in less-controlled capture conditions.

Some evaluation design choices (thresholds for region merging/matching, aggregation into scene-level tracks, asymmetric geometry rule) are somewhat heuristic; although sensitivity analysis is provided and shows general stability, the chosen operating points and their generality to unseen domains are not deeply theoretically justified.

Dataset scale (350 pairs, ~1000 annotated objects) is modest by broader CV benchmark standards, and about 43% of the pairs (150) are drawn from an existing HD-Epic dataset rather than newly collected, somewhat limiting the novelty of the data diversity claim relative to the 200 self-collected pairs.

Only a single VLM baseline (Qwen2.5-VL + SAM3) is evaluated; comparisons against other recent multimodal/VLM-based reasoning approaches for change description would strengthen the claim of large relative improvement over 'existing approaches.'
